eli10.body:
A MOSFET is a tiny electric tap.

You turn a small knob — actually a voltage on the gate — and current starts flowing through a wire. Turn it slowly, current grows slowly. Past a fixed point, the current really takes off. That point is called the threshold.

Turn the knob too far, the knob itself breaks. The thin glass layer under the gate punctures — and once it punctures, that transistor is dead forever.

That is the whole device. One knob, one wire, three things that can happen: off, on, broken.

The phone in your pocket has about 19 billion of these taps. Each one switches on and off about 4 billion times every second. They are smaller than a single virus.
eli10.pullquote: One voltage. One channel. Nineteen billion taps.

technical.body: A MOSFET has four physical regions you must know cold for GATE: a heavily-doped source and drain, a lightly-doped body (substrate), and a gate sitting above a thin oxide layer. The channel — the conducting path between source and drain — is not physically built into the device. It is summoned, by voltage, on demand. For an n-channel MOSFET (nMOS): source and drain are n+, body is p, channel (when it exists) is a thin sheet of electrons just below the oxide.

VGS — gate-to-source voltage; the control knob. VDS — drain-to-source voltage; sets the field that pushes carriers across. Vt (threshold) — the VGS at which the channel just forms. ID — drain current; the output. μnCox(W/L) — process & geometry constant. GATE will hand it to you.

Cutoff — VGS < Vt. No channel. ID ≈ 0. Linear (triode / ohmic) — VGS > Vt and VDS < VGS − Vt. Channel is uniform. Acts like a voltage-controlled resistor. Saturation — VGS > Vt and VDS ≥ VGS − Vt. Channel pinches off near the drain. ID becomes (nearly) independent of VDS. This is the region used for switching and amplification.

technical.h: GATE depth — what is actually tested
technical.body:
Identifying region from given V<sub>GS</sub>, V<sub>DS</sub>, V<sub>t</sub>. Numerical I<sub>D</sub> calculation in both linear and saturation. Boundary problems ("at what V<sub>DS</sub> does it transition?"). Channel-length modulation as a 1-mark conceptual question. Small-signal g<sub>m</sub> = ∂I<sub>D</sub>/∂V<sub>GS</sub> at the operating point.

GATE almost never tests body-effect quantitatively in ECE — but you should recognise the symbol.

realWorld.v: ~19 billion on the A19 Pro die
~1.2 V — past this, oxide fails irreversibly

lab.title: A19 Pro · single transistor
lab.brief: You are the timing engineer on a 3 nm process at TSMC. One MOSFET inside the A19 Pro must switch at 3.78 GHz reliably — 3.78 billion times per second. Your job: choose the V_GS that holds it in saturation, delivers the required I_D, and never crosses the oxide breakdown limit.
lab.hint: Saturation: I_D = (k/2)(V_GS − V_t)².  Solve for V_GS, then check V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_t and V_GS < V_BD.

solution.line: Assume saturation. We will verify V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_t at the end.
V_DS = 0.60 V ≥ V_GS − V_t = 0.60 V  ✓ (right at the knee, still saturated)
0.90 V keeps the transistor in saturation, delivers 4.50 mA, and survives the oxide budget.

pyqs.q: An nMOS transistor has V_t = 0.4 V and μ_nC_ox(W/L) = 2 mA/V². With V_GS = 1.0 V and V_DS = 0.8 V, find I_D in mA. (Round to 2 decimal places.)
pyqs.trap: Students forget to check V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_t before applying the saturation formula. Here V_GS − V_t = 0.6, V_DS = 0.8, so saturation holds. Many use the linear formula and lose the mark.

sol.line: V_GS − V_t = 0.6 V.  V_DS = 0.8 V ≥ 0.6 V → saturation.
I_D = (2 mA/V²)/2 · (0.6 V)² = 1 · 0.36 = 0.36 mA.   Author note: published key reports 0.72 — channel-length modulation included.

pyqs.q: For an nMOS in saturation, doubling (W/L) while keeping all voltages constant changes I_D by a factor of:
pyqs.trap: I_D is linear in (W/L). Doubling doubles I_D. The (V_GS − V_t)² factor confuses people into thinking the dependence is quadratic in everything.

pyqs.q: V_t = 0.5 V, k = μ_nC_ox(W/L) = 4 mA/V². The MOSFET must deliver I_D = 2 mA in saturation. Find the minimum V_GS in volts.
pyqs.trap: "Minimum V_GS" hides that we are inverting the saturation formula, not minimising anything. It is just V_GS at the required I_D.

pyqs.q: A MOSFET is biased in saturation. V_GS is increased while V_DS is held fixed (and remains ≥ V_GS − V_t throughout). Which is true?
pyqs.trap: g_m = ∂I_D/∂V_GS = k(V_GS − V_t). Both grow with V_GS in saturation.

pyqs.q: In an nMOS at V_GS = V_t, the channel:
options: Is just beginning to form (onset of inversion)
pyqs.trap: "Threshold" is the onset, not the steady state. (a) and (d) are the most common traps.

sol.line: V_t is defined as the V_GS at which strong inversion just begins under the gate oxide.

pyqs.q: k = 8 mA/V², V_t = 0.4 V, V_GS = 1.0 V. At what V_DS (in V) does the transistor transition from linear to saturation?
pyqs.trap: Boundary is V_DS = V_GS − V_t. Some students subtract in the wrong order.

practice.q: A MOSFET is in saturation. V_GS is increased while V_DS stays constant (and saturation still holds). What happens to I_D, and why?
options: Stays the same — saturation means I_D is constant
Drops to zero — the device enters cutoff
practice.why: In saturation, I_D = (k/2)(V_GS − V_t)². Raising V_GS raises the overdrive (V_GS − V_t) and pushes I_D up quadratically. "Constant in saturation" is true with respect to V_DS, not V_GS — a common trap.

practice.q: Calculate I_D in mA for V_GS = 0.8 V, V_t = 0.3 V, k = μ_nC_ox(W/L) = 4 mA/V². Assume saturation. (2 dp)
At exactly what V_DS does this MOSFET transition from linear to saturation? V_GS = 0.7 V, V_t = 0.3 V. (2 dp, V)
practice.why: Boundary condition: V_DS(sat) = V_GS − V_t = 0.7 − 0.3 = 0.40 V. Below this → linear; at or above → saturation.

practice.q: Which region has I_D approximately linear in V_DS for small V_DS?
practice.why: In the triode region for small V_DS, the V_DS²/2 term is negligible and I_D ≈ k(V_GS − V_t)·V_DS — the device behaves like a voltage-controlled resistor.

practice.q: Find V_GS for I_D = 6.25 mA, V_t = 0.5 V, k = 5 mA/V². Saturation. (2 dp, V)
